column1: What is the end-to-end principle, as articulated by Saltzer, Reed, and Clark (1984)?
column2: The network should only route packets between addresses; all other properties (reliability, ordering, flow control, error correction) are the responsibility of the endpoints, not the network core.

column1: How many layers does the TCP/IP model use compared to the OSI model, and which OSI layers disappear?
column2: TCP/IP collapses the 7 OSI layers into 4 (Link, Internet, Transport, Application). The Session and Presentation layers disappear, absorbed into the application or simply omitted.

column1: Why is IP classified as a 'best-effort, connectionless' protocol?
column2: IP makes no delivery guarantees: it does not retransmit lost packets, does not reorder out-of-order arrivals, and does not notify the sender of congestion—reliability is pushed to endpoint protocols like TCP.

column1: Why can't flat MAC addressing scale for internet-wide routing?
column2: MAC addresses are random 48-bit identifiers with no topological information, forcing routers to maintain an O(N) complete mapping of every address to every segment, which is untenable at internet scale.

column1: What problem does hierarchical IP addressing (network + host portions) solve for routers?
column2: It allows routers to make forwarding decisions based on aggregated address prefixes (via CIDR) rather than individual host entries, compressing routing tables from billions of entries to hundreds of thousands of prefixes.

column1: What three forces caused IPv4 address exhaustion despite its theoretical 4.29 billion address space?
column2: 1) Profligate early allocations (e.g., MIT, IBM, Ford each received full /8 blocks of 16.7M addresses), 2) rigid classful addressing (Class A/B/C) causing internal fragmentation, 3) explosive growth of internet-connected devices.

column1: What is the role of TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers?
column2: Sequence numbers (from a random 32-bit initial value) let the receiver detect gaps, duplicates, and reordering; acknowledgment numbers tell the sender which bytes were successfully delivered, driving retransmission of lost data.

column1: Distinguish TCP flow control from congestion control.
column2: Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver via an advertised receive window bounding in-flight unacknowledged data. Congestion control addresses shared network resource contention, inferring capacity from loss/RTT signals and adjusting the congestion window to avoid congestion collapse.

column1: What invariant must a TCP sender always respect regarding the receiver's advertised window?
column2: The sender must never transmit more unacknowledged data than the receiver's advertised receive window, regardless of its own sending capacity.

column1: What is the 'narrow waist' of the TCP/IP hourglass architecture?
column2: IP sits at the narrow waist as a connectionless, best-effort packet delivery service; all link-layer technologies converge below it, and all transport/application protocols (TCP, UDP, HTTP, DNS, QUIC) build above it, forming the universal interoperability contract.

column1: Why does DNS use UDP while HTTP uses TCP?
column2: DNS queries are small, idempotent, single-round-trip with no need for connection state—UDP with application-level retransmission suffices. HTTP requires ordered, complete delivery of arbitrarily large payloads, which TCP's byte-stream, handshake, and acknowledgment mechanisms provide.

column1: Why can't DHCP use TCP for its initial host configuration exchange?
column2: DHCP must operate before the host has an IP address, and TCP requires an established connection between two known addressed endpoints, making TCP unusable prior to address assignment.
